reference.source: Kelley and Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology
clinicalPearls: Cryoglobulins are immunoglobulins that precipitate reversibly below core body temperature; the resulting immune-complex deposition drives a small-vessel vasculitis.
The classic clinical triad is palpable purpura of the lower limbs, arthralgia and fatigue (Meltzer triad), often with peripheral neuropathy.
Type II (mixed monoclonal IgM with rheumatoid factor activity plus polyclonal IgG) is the commonest vasculitic type and is strongly linked to chronic hepatitis C.

Type I cryoglobulinaemia (single monoclonal immunoglobulin) reflects an underlying lymphoproliferative or plasma-cell disorder and tends to cause hyperviscosity and occlusive acral ischaemia rather than classic vasculitis.
Low C4 with relatively preserved C3 is a characteristic complement pattern; rheumatoid factor is typically positive.
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is the dominant renal lesion and a major determinant of long-term outcome.
Correct sampling is essential: blood must be collected and transported at 37 degrees Celsius or the cryoglobulin may be missed (false negative).
Treatment addresses the underlying cause (antiviral therapy for hepatitis C, B-cell depletion for severe or refractory disease) rather than immunosuppression alone.
reference.pathophysiology: Cryoglobulins are circulating immunoglobulins that undergo reversible precipitation at temperatures below 37 degrees Celsius. In mixed (type II and type III) disease a chronic antigenic stimulus, most often hepatitis C virus, drives expansion of rheumatoid-factor-producing B cells; the resulting IgM-IgG immune complexes deposit in small vessel walls, activate the classical complement pathway and recruit neutrophils, producing a leukocytoclastic small-vessel vasculitis. In type I disease a monoclonal immunoglobulin from an underlying B-cell or plasma-cell clone precipitates and occludes vessels, causing hyperviscosity and thrombotic acral ischaemia. Cold exposure promotes precipitation, explaining the distal, cool, dependent distribution of skin lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Septic vasculitis or infective endocarditis with embolic purpura
additionalInvestigations: Serum cryoglobulin assay with cryocrit, using strict 37 degrees Celsius collection and transport
Hepatitis C serology and HCV RNA, plus hepatitis B and HIV testing
Complement levels (characteristically low C4, relatively preserved C3) and rheumatoid factor
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to detect a monoclonal component
Renal function, urinalysis and urine protein quantification for glomerulonephritis
Skin or renal biopsy demonstrating immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis
Nerve conduction studies where peripheral neuropathy is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine or heavy proteinuria
Digital or acral necrosis and impending gangrene
Mononeuritis multiplex or rapidly progressive sensorimotor neuropathy
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage or gastrointestinal ischaemia
Hyperviscosity features (visual disturbance, confusion, mucosal bleeding) suggesting type I disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause and on renal and neurological involvement; hepatitis C-associated disease often improves markedly with sustained virological clearance. Severe renal disease, extensive vasculitic ulceration or an underlying malignant lymphoproliferative disorder carry a worse outlook.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis because blood was not kept at 37 degrees Celsius, giving a false-negative cryoglobulin result.
Attributing purpura to simple hypersensitivity and failing to screen for hepatitis C and an underlying B-cell clone.
Immunosuppressing hepatitis C-driven disease without concurrent antiviral therapy, risking viral flare.
Overlooking type I cryoglobulinaemia as a marker of occult myeloma, Waldenstroem macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma.
Interpreting a normal C3 as excluding active disease when the key finding is a disproportionately low C4.

Oxford Textbook of Medicine, current edition

management: Treat the underlying driver, using direct-acting antiviral therapy to achieve sustained virological clearance in hepatitis C-associated mixed cryoglobulinaemia
For severe or organ-threatening disease, induce remission with B-cell depletion using rituximab together with corticosteroids
In rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, hyperviscosity or extensive vasculitic ulceration, add plasma exchange and pulsed corticosteroids
For type I disease, treat the underlying lymphoproliferative or plasma-cell clone with directed chemo-immunotherapy
Provide supportive care including cold avoidance, analgesia for arthralgia and neuropathy, and wound care for skin ulceration
Monitor renal function, urinalysis, complement levels and cryocrit to track disease activity
Coordinate care across rheumatology, hepatology, nephrology and haematology
